magazine.name: At Home
magazine.coverline: Six small tools, built after hours.
letter: Most of the software in my life wants something from me: an account, a subscription, a line to someone else's server. The things I build after hours go the other way.

This first issue collects six of them. A journal for difficult days that nobody else can read. A viewer for drone flight logs. A bridge between my training log and an AI coach. A bookshelf and a budget that live in my notes, and a dictation app that never sends a word anywhere.
All of them are open source and free. If one is useful to you, take it. If something breaks, tell me on GitHub.

projects.headline: A journal that stays yours.
projects.blurb: A private, offline journal for mood, events, fears, sleep and nightmares, built with particular care for people going through a hard time and for people who see a therapist.
story: Most journaling apps start by asking for an account. Mossbook has no server to make one on. Entries are encrypted on the device, the app never connects to the internet, and even updates are something you go and fetch yourself.

It knows six kinds of entries: mood on a scale of one to five with emotions, events, fears and triggers with their intensity before and after a coping strategy, sleep, nightmares with a rewritten version, and free notes. A quick entry takes at most two taps and can be finished later. Over time, the Patterns view shows mood, a mood calendar and overviews, written as plain observations rather than clinical conclusions.

For the hardest moments there is a plan you write yourself, with crisis numbers and grounding exercises available without unlocking. And when there is something to bring to a session, Mossbook makes a PDF report for a chosen period, optionally protected with a password.

projects.headline: Replay every DJI flight in 3D.
projects.blurb: Drop the FlightRecord folder from your phone or controller onto the page and every flight appears on a map, replayed over real terrain and buildings.
story: DJI drones keep a detailed log of every flight. Drone Log Visualizer turns that folder into something you can actually look at. Drop the whole FlightRecord folder onto the page: duplicates are skipped, errors are grouped by cause, and you get totals per aircraft.

Each flight replays as a ribbon at real height over terrain, 3D buildings and woods, colored by height, speed or battery. Charts for height, speed, battery, GPS satellites, gimbal pitch and signal move in sync with the map. Drag to zoom, click to jump, play back at up to fifty times the speed. In Poland it can even fetch the height of every tree and building from airborne laser scanning.

It reads every log format from v1 to v14, including encrypted logs from current DJI apps with your own free developer key. Everything runs in one Docker container and stays in a local database, with export to CSV, GPX and KML.

projects.title: Intervals.icu MCP
projects.headline: Talk to your training log.
projects.blurb: Connects Claude and other AI assistants to Intervals.icu, so they can read your activities, fitness and wellness, and help you plan what comes next.
story: Intervals.icu knows everything about your training. This server lets an AI assistant know it too. Claude Desktop, Claude Code, Cursor, VS Code or any other MCP client can read your activities, fitness, wellness and calendar, and help plan the weeks ahead.

It has 47 hand-designed tools, grouped into toolsets you can switch on and off so the model's context isn't flooded, and all 149 Intervals.icu API operations are accounted for. The client is generated from the official OpenAPI spec, and pace comes out the way runners read it, in min/km or min/mi with GAP and zones.

It is careful by default. Tools for deleting aren't even registered unless you ask for them, planned workouts are checked after saving, and duplicate events are skipped. Ready-made prompts cover a weekly review, a recovery check and planning next week.

projects.headline: Your bookshelf, as plain Markdown.
projects.blurb: A personal library inside Obsidian that syncs with your notes and works offline on desktop and mobile.
story: Shelfmark turns an Obsidian vault into a personal library. Every book is a plain Markdown note with its data in properties, and covers are saved in the vault, so the library travels with the rest of your notes and keeps working without a connection.

Books come in by title, author or ISBN from Open Library, Google Books and, optionally, the National Library of Poland. The library shows covers or a list, with status tabs, filters and ready-made shelves: owned but unread, wishlist, favorites, on loan. There is a reading queue, a yearly goal, reading progress, loans in both directions with reminders, and a wishlist you can export as gift ideas.

If Claude Code is installed, Shelfmark can use it for book suggestions, a reading profile, a pick of what to read next from your own shelves, and a recap of earlier volumes before the next book in a series. All of it is optional.

projects.headline: Dictate anywhere. Nothing leaves the phone.
projects.blurb: On-device speech-to-text, one tap away in Quick Settings.
story: Voicemator puts dictation in Android's Quick Settings. Pull down the shade, tap Dictate, speak, tap again, and the text is on the clipboard. Turn on the optional accessibility service and a small mic button appears at the keyboard instead, typing straight into the field you're editing.

Speech never leaves the phone. It runs Parakeet Ultra, a post-trained version of NVIDIA's Parakeet covering 25 European languages, entirely on the device after a one-time model download. Long dictations are transcribed in the background while you speak, so the text is ready the moment you stop.

Around that sit the details: a dictionary for names it gets wrong, app profiles with no full stop in messengers and full punctuation in email, a filter for hesitation sounds, and transcription of voice messages and audio files of any length.

features: Quick Settings tile, widget or a mic button at the keyboard
History and stats, kept on the phone

projects.title: Caishen
projects.headline: Your budget, next to your notes.
projects.blurb: A budget tracker that lives in your Obsidian vault, with a dashboard that shows where the money goes.
story: Caishen, named after the Chinese god of wealth, is a budget tracker that lives inside your Obsidian vault, right next to the rest of your notes. There is no separate app and no account to sign up for.

A dashboard shows the month's income, expenses and balance at a glance. Monthly budgets per category show how much is left, recurring payments such as rent or subscriptions are entered once, and savings goals track progress toward a target.
Five tabs, Overview, Categories, Goals, Analytics and Transactions, cover the rest, with yearly overviews and trends over the last months. Categories, currency and language are all yours to set.
